title: One flash of anger
hookLine: a pan of oil left a moment too long, and the smell of smoke; Shantideva opens his chapter on patience with fire
tomorrow: if it can be fixed, why worry? and if it can't?

lines: HOW MUCH CAN ONE FLASH BURN?
cards: Anyone who's cooked knows the smell. Oil in a pan, left one moment too long while you answered a text. First a shimmer, then a thin gray thread of smoke, and then, faster than seems fair, a flame.

A kitchen that took years to make into a home can be blackened in a minute. So how much good can a single flash of anger burn? Shantideva answers on the very first line of chapter six, and his answer is fire.

teach.b: Here's the opening, close to his words. All the good you've gathered over ages and ages, generosity, honoring the Buddhas, every kind act, one moment of anger can destroy.
Then the next verse: there is no wrong like hatred, and no discipline like patience. It's meant to land like heat on the skin. Not a slow fade.
A flash. And he keeps going, almost like a doctor listing symptoms.
Someone gripped by anger finds no peace of mind, no joy, no ease. Sleep won't come. Even people who depend on their kindness may turn against them.
Notice where the fire burns first. Not mostly the other person. It burns the one holding it.

So the work of patience begins in a very physical place: the warmth in the face, the tight jaw, the heat rising in the chest. That's the smoke before the flame. You don't have to win an argument with the anger.

teach.h: NOTICE THE SHIMMER IN THE PAN.
teach.b: You just need to notice the shimmer in the pan, early, while turning down the heat is still easy.
One flash burns much. One noticed flash burns much less.

how: Mahayana Buddhists study Shantideva's sixth chapter as a core teaching on patience (kshanti), and Tibetan teachers often open lessons on anger with its first verses.

games.q: what does “one flash of anger” mean?
o: a burst of light seen at the moment of awakening
a quick temper that's harmless once it's over
a moment of anger that can burn up much good

games.q: chapter six's fire — tap the pairs.
p: can destroy good gathered over ages
no peace, no joy, no sleep
heat in the face, a tight jaw

s: anger mostly harms the person it's aimed at
Shantideva lists what it does to the one holding it: no peace, no joy, no sleep.
Shantideva says there's no discipline like patience
it's the second verse of the chapter: no wrong like hatred, no discipline like patience.

games.q: your dad cuts you off mid-sentence at dinner, again, and you feel your face go hot. you've got about a second. what's the chapter-six move?
o: let it out now; holding anger in is what really hurts you.
notice the heat, the shimmer in the pan, and turn it down before it flames.
pretend nothing happened and change the subject cheerfully.
games.why: Shantideva's patience starts with noticing the heat early. it isn't pretending, and it isn't letting the flash burn.

practice: Rub your palms together fast, about ten times, until they're warm. Then hold them still, an inch apart, and feel the heat. Stay with that warmth as it slowly fades, the way a flash of anger fades when nothing is added to it.

wordCard.voice: One flash of anger: chapter six's opening warning. A moment of hatred can burn up a great deal of good, beginning with your own peace.

orig.note: Sanskrit: anger, wrath. Chapter six names it among the strongest forces patience meets.

carryVoice: Carry this one: one flash burns much, so watch for the shimmer in the pan. Patience has begun.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 6.1-6.5 (a single moment of hatred destroys good deeds gathered over eons; there is no evil like hatred and no austerity like patience; the angry find no peace, joy or sleep; even dependents may turn on them)
